In the small town of Wardha, news travels fast, and Kalyani's sister-in-law brought hers over with the evening tea.
"Every night Anand goes to the terrace with his phone for an hour. And he's always writing in that notebook. Aren't you worried?"
Kalyani stirred her tea. She had noticed too. For a moment the old sick feeling rose in her chest. Then she thought of what she knew: since his father died in March, Anand had grown quieter, and he still called his mother every night. The notebook he had kept since college.
"He's allowed some things that are just his," she said.
That night, she didn't check the notebook. She only asked, "Is anything worrying you that affects us?"
Anand looked surprised, then sat down. "I've been writing about Baba. I wasn't ready to share it. But nothing is wrong between us. I promise."
Kalyani nodded, and believed him.

Deepak's chin wobbled. "I kicked the ball there."
"Thank you for telling me. That's more important than a pot."
They swept up the pieces together. I couldn't hear the rest, but Deepak ran back to his ball, smiling.

qa.q: What lay in pieces by Deepak's ball?
qa.a: A clay pot lay in pieces.

qa.q: How did Deepak seem to feel right after the crash?
qa.a: Deepak seemed frightened and unsure, freezing after the crash, then relieved after he confessed.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do instead of shouting?
qa.a: He crouched, named the broken pot, invited Deepak to help clean it, and thanked him for telling the truth.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Jagdish's response?
qa.a: The neighbour finds it memorable and warm, though they could not hear everything, noticing Deepak ran back smiling.

grounding: A neighbour observes a father avoiding a trap question, thanking his young son for confessing, and calmly repairing the broken pot together.

At the parent-teacher meeting, the class teacher pushed Pranav's English notebook toward Arnab. "Your son writes that he rode a dragon to school on Monday. And last week he said he has a friend who lives in the water tank. He is lying in his compositions."
Arnab turned the pages. There was the dragon, drawn in red pen, with Pranav on its back holding his tiffin.
He felt a flash of irritation, and then something protective. He remembered Pranav whispering about the water-tank friend at bedtime, eyes bright.
"Ma'am, the prompt said 'My journey to school.' He knows he didn't ride a dragon. That's imagination, not lying."
The teacher paused. "Perhaps he could label it a story."
"That's fair. I'll help him write 'my pretend journey' at the top."
At home, Pranav asked anxiously, "Am I in trouble?"
"No," Arnab said. "Your dragon is brilliant."

qa.q: What did Pranav write that he rode to school?
qa.a: He wrote that he rode a dragon to school on Monday.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel as he looked at the dragon drawing?
qa.a: Arnab felt a flash of irritation, then protective, remembering Pranav's bright eyes and seeing the story as healthy imagination.

qa.q: What small step did Arnab agree to that respected both the teacher and Pranav?
qa.a: He agreed to help Pranav write "my pretend journey" at the top, so the story is clearly labelled without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt if he had been called a liar for the dragon?
qa.a: Pranav would likely feel ashamed of his imagination and might stop sharing his stories, since he was already anxious about being in trouble.

grounding: It shows a father seeing his son's dragon story called a lie and recognising it as normal pretend play that should not be shamed.

I sit on the bench in the park every evening, so I've watched Sarika and her son Kishore for months. I can't know what goes on in her head, but I can tell you what I see.
Kishore talks to someone called Bholu who nobody else can see. Bholu sits on the swing next to him. Bholu is afraid of dogs.
One evening, another mother laughed and said, "Your son is telling lies already?" Sarika's face went tight for a second. Then she said, "No. Bholu is his friend. Kishore, does Bholu want a push?"
Kishore beamed. "Bholu wants a big push!"
Sarika pushed the empty swing. Kishore laughed so hard he nearly fell off his own.
Later I heard her tell him, "You know Bholu is pretend, na?" He said, "Yes, Mumma. But pretend is real in my head." She kissed his head and said, "That's exactly right."

qa.q: What is Bholu afraid of?
qa.a: Bholu is afraid of dogs.

qa.q: What does Sarika's face going tight suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Sarika felt stung and briefly defensive when her son was called a liar, before choosing to protect his play.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that respected Kishore's imagination?
qa.a: She refused to call it lying, played along by pushing the empty swing, and later checked gently that he knew Bholu was pretend.

qa.q: How does Kishore feel when his mother pushes Bholu's swing?
qa.a: Kishore feels delighted and understood, beaming and laughing so hard he nearly falls.

grounding: A park regular observes a mother seeing her son's invisible friend called a lie, and treating it as healthy pretend play instead.

Monday. At breakfast, Ganga announced that she had flown to the moon in the night and eaten a rasgulla there. Vandana, her mother, opened her mouth to say, "Don't tell lies," then stopped. Ganga's eyes were shining.
Wednesday. Nani was visiting. Ganga told her about the moon rasgulla. Nani frowned. "Chhi, a girl who tells lies grows a long nose." Ganga went red and quiet, and didn't tell another story all day. Vandana noticed, and felt a tight knot in her stomach.
Saturday. At bedtime, Vandana said, "Ganga, what else happened on the moon?" Ganga looked at her carefully. "It's pretend, Ma." "I know. I love pretend. Tell me."
Ganga sat up, beaming. "There was a cat who drove a bus."

qa.q: What did Ganga say she ate on the moon?
qa.a: She said she ate a rasgulla there.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when Ganga went quiet after Nani's remark?
qa.a: Vandana felt a tight knot of worry, seeing that being called a liar had shamed Ganga's imagination.

qa.q: What did Vandana do on Saturday that helped?
qa.a: She asked for more of the moon story and said she loved pretend, showing Ganga her imagination was welcome.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel when her mother asks for more?
qa.a: Ganga feels relieved and happy, sitting up and beaming, after checking her mother knows it is pretend.

grounding: It shows a mother noticing over several days how calling pretend stories lies shames her daughter, and choosing to welcome the imagination.

The power went out in the middle of the Class 5 half-yearly exam, and the room went dim. In the confusion, Naveen knocked over his ink bottle. It splashed across the answer sheet of the boy next to him.
Siddharth Sir walked over with his torch. "Who spilled this?"
Naveen's mouth went dry. A month ago, when he had confessed to breaking the class globe, Siddharth Sir had made him stand on the bench for the whole period while the class laughed. He still remembered every face.
"I don't know, Sir," Naveen said. "It was dark."
His neighbour stared at him. Naveen stared at his paper. His hands were shaking.
He knew he was lying. He also knew, very clearly, that the truth had cost him more last time. That evening he told his mother everything, crying, and she said she would speak to the principal the next morning.

qa.q: What did Naveen knock over?
qa.a: He knocked over his ink bottle.

qa.q: Why did Naveen say "I don't know, Sir"?
qa.a: Naveen felt afraid of being humiliated again, because the last time he told the truth he was made to stand on the bench while the class laughed.

qa.q: What could make it safer for Naveen to tell the truth in class?
qa.a: If Sir responded to confessions calmly and privately instead of shaming, and with his mother and the principal involved, Naveen would learn truth is safe.

qa.q: How might Naveen's neighbour feel when Naveen says he doesn't know?
qa.a: The neighbour probably feels angry and unfairly treated, staring at Naveen because his answer sheet is ruined.

grounding: It shows a child who was humiliated for confessing now lying out of fear under pressure, learning that lying feels safer than truth.

Last month, when Nandini admitted she had left her tiffin box on the school bus, her mother put Mahima Masi on speakerphone at dinner and told the whole story. "Our careless donkey loses everything!" Everyone laughed. Nandini laughed too, then cried in the bathroom.
Now, on Saturday, Nandini was alone in the living room when Masi's reading glasses slid off the sofa and cracked under her foot.
Her heart pounded.
She pushed the glasses under the cushion.
When Masi asked, "Has anyone seen my glasses?", Nandini said, "No, Masi," and went to her room. She sat on her bed, feeling sick. It was that telling the truth had been worse.
Later that evening, Masi knocked gently and sat with her. "Whatever happened, I won't laugh. I promise." Nandini burst into tears and told her.

qa.q: Why did Nandini hide the glasses?
qa.a: Nandini felt afraid of being humiliated again at dinner, since last time her honesty led to laughter and being called a donkey.

qa.q: What did Masi do that made the truth feel safe?

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother feel if she understood why Nandini hid the glasses?
qa.a: She might feel sorry and a bit ashamed, realising the joke at dinner taught Nandini that truth brings humiliation.

grounding: It shows a child who was mocked for confessing learning to hide a mistake, until an adult makes the truth safe.

"Bidisha, why did you tell Baba your uniform tore on the bus door?" Harsha asked, sitting on the stairs of their building. "I saw you catch it on the gate while climbing."
Bidisha twisted the torn sleeve. "Because."
"Because what?"
"Last time I told Baba the truth about breaking the flowerpot, he made me go to every flat and say sorry. Everyone laughed. The aunties called me 'flowerpot' for weeks."
"That sounds horrible."
"So now I just say something else. It's easier."
Harsha was quiet. "Do you like lying?"

"What if I come with you and we tell Baba together? I'll ask him not to make it a show."
Bidisha looked up. "Will he listen to you?"

I live next door to Rafiq and his son Chetan, and the walls are thin.
On Tuesday evening Rafiq's phone rang. I heard him say, "Tell them I'm not home," and Chetan, who is about nine, answered and said, "Abbu isn't home." Then a small pause. "Abbu, you are home."
Later I saw them on the balcony. I couldn't hear all of it, and I don't know what Rafiq was thinking. But I heard him say, "You're right. I made you lie for me. That was wrong." Chetan asked why he did it. Rafiq said, "I didn't want to talk to my boss. That's not a good reason."
The next morning I heard Rafiq on the phone again, loud enough through the wall: "Sir, yesterday I asked my son to say I wasn't home. I was. I'm sorry." Chetan was standing right beside him.

qa.q: What did Rafiq ask Chetan to say on the phone?
qa.a: Tell them I'm not home.

qa.q: How did Rafiq seem to feel on the balcony?
qa.a: Rafiq seemed ashamed and regretful, admitting he had made his son lie for him and that his reason was not good.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that teaches honesty better than a lecture?
qa.a: He openly owned his error to Chetan and then called his boss to admit the truth while Chetan stood beside him.

qa.q: How might Chetan see his father's phone call the next morning?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels proud and learns that adults fix their mistakes too, not just children.

grounding: A neighbour observes a father who made his son tell a white lie on the phone owning the error openly, modelling honesty.

Friday. On the city bus, the conductor asked Shankar's age. His mother Vasudha said, "Five," though he was seven, to avoid buying his ticket. Shankar stared at her.
Sunday. At the fair, the ticket counter asked Shankar's age for the ride. "Five," he said confidently. Vasudha went red. "He's seven," she told the attendant, and paid.
Later, on the walk home, Shankar asked, "Why was it wrong for me? You said five on the bus."
Vasudha stopped under a streetlight. Her cheeks burned. "You're right. I did it first. It was wrong when I did it too." She took his hand.
Tuesday. On the bus again, the conductor asked. Before Shankar could speak, Vasudha said, "He's seven. One full, one child," and counted out the coins. She glanced at Shankar. He smiled, a little surprised, and sat up very straight.

qa.q: How old was Shankar really?
qa.a: He was seven.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when Shankar asked why it was wrong for him?
qa.a: Vasudha felt ashamed and embarrassed, her cheeks burning, because she saw he had copied her own dishonesty.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that taught honesty best?
qa.a: She admitted to Shankar that she did it first and it was wrong, then showed it by paying the correct fare on Tuesday.

qa.q: How does Shankar react when his mother tells the truth on Tuesday?
qa.a: Shankar feels surprised and proud, smiling and sitting up very straight.

grounding: It shows a child copying his mother's small dishonesty and the mother owning her error openly, teaching more than a lecture.
